name: Butler Lampson
milestone_by_age_26: As a Project GENIE member at UC Berkeley, helped develop the Berkeley Timesharing System for the SDS 940 around 1965 (age 21); completed a Berkeley PhD in EECS in 1967 (age 23) and became an assistant professor the same year.
early_history_summary: Lampson graduated from the Lawrenceville School, earned an A.B. in physics magna cum laude from Harvard in 1964 at about age 20, then moved into systems research at UC Berkeley's Project GENIE. By his early twenties he was a core contributor to the SDS 940 timesharing system and finished a PhD under Harry Huskey in 1967, immediately joining Berkeley's faculty.
family_context_summary: Born December 23, 1943 in Washington, D.C. Early family financial or parental domain details are not documented in reviewed sources; education path ran through elite preparatory school and Harvard.
evidence_summary: Lampson entered systems research at the frontier of interactive computing via Harvard physics and Berkeley Project GENIE, contributing to the Berkeley Timesharing System for the SDS 940 by about age 21 and earning a PhD plus assistant professorship by 23. Elite prep school, Harvard, Berkeley, and collaborators such as Peter Deutsch concentrated opportunity. Family domain advantage is not documented; later Xerox PARC work (Alto, Ethernet-related systems) after age 26 cemented a Turing Award-level career.
starting_point: Born 1943 in Washington, D.C.; elite preparatory education at Lawrenceville School before Harvard physics.
current_position: Turing Award-winning computer scientist; long affiliated with Microsoft Research as a Technical Fellow and MIT as adjunct professor; living as of mid-2020s.

trajectory.event: Earned A.B. in physics magna cum laude from Harvard University.
Helped develop the Berkeley Timesharing System for the SDS 940 as part of Project GENIE.
Completed PhD in EECS at UC Berkeley and joined the Berkeley faculty as assistant professor.
Became a founding member of Xerox PARC's Computer Science Laboratory.
Wrote the influential 'Why Alto?' memo articulating a personal computer vision.
Contributed to the Xerox Alto, widely regarded as a foundational personal computer with GUI-style interaction.
Received the ACM Turing Award for contributions to personal distributed computing.
Joined Microsoft Research as an architect (later Distinguished Engineer and Technical Fellow).

name: Ralph H. Baer
milestone_by_age_26: Major material milestone (home video game console / Magnavox Odyssey work from ~1966–1972) occurred in his mid-40s to age 50; by age 26 he had radio technician training and WWII service but no independently celebrated invention or founding event.
early_history_summary: German-born Jewish refugee who trained as a radio service technician (1940), served in U.S. military intelligence in WWII, and earned a B.S. in television engineering in 1949 (age 27). He later conceived TV games at Sanders Associates and licensed the Brown Box to Magnavox as the Odyssey.
family_context_summary: Born Rudolf Heinrich Baer in 1922 in Germany to a Jewish family; father worked in a shoe factory. Family fled Nazi Germany to New York in 1938.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Leo Baer worked in a shoe factory; no documented computer or electronics domain apprenticeship from parents.
evidence_summary: Baer's defining achievement—the Brown Box / Magnavox Odyssey—came decades after age 26. Early radio technician graduation and wartime service do not meet the bar for a material success-by-26 milestone under a conservative reading.

name: Henriette Avram
milestone_by_age_26: Defining MARC work began at the Library of Congress in 1965 when she was about 45–46; earlier programming at NSA started around age 32–33, well after age 26.
early_history_summary: Born Henriette Regina Davidson in New York in 1919, she studied pre-med at Hunter College, married in 1941, and later studied mathematics at George Washington University. She joined the NSA as an early computer programmer in 1952 and moved to the Library of Congress in 1965 to create MARC.
family_context_summary: Born in Manhattan in 1919; father was a watch material distributor and mother a newspaper reporter.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents worked in distribution and journalism, not computing; computing career began after marriage and homemaking years.
evidence_summary: MARC development (1965–late 1960s) and NSA programming (from 1952) both occurred well after age 26; no material dated milestone by age 26 found.

name: William N. Carrico Jr.
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Bridge Communications in 1981 at about age 31; by age 26 he had a BSEE (1972) and early Fairchild/Zilog industry roles, but no material founding or invention milestone by 26 was found.
early_history_summary: Born February 12, 1950, Carrico grew up partly in Montana and Sunnyvale, earned a BSEE from Santa Clara University in 1972, worked at Fairchild Semiconductor and Zilog, then co-founded Bridge Communications with Judith Estrin in 1981 (later 3Com, Cisco, Packet Design roles).
evidence_summary: Bridge Communications founding at age ~31 is the first clear material entrepreneurial milestone; pre-26 path is standard engineering education and early industry jobs.

name: Tim Berners-Lee
category: Computer scientist / World Wide Web inventor
milestone_by_age_26: While a contractor at CERN in 1980 (age 25), proposed a hypertext information-sharing system and built the ENQUIRE prototype, the direct conceptual precursor to the World Wide Web.
early_history_summary: Born in London to computer pioneers who worked on the Ferranti Mark 1, Berners-Lee attended Emanuel School and earned a first-class physics degree from Queen's College, Oxford in 1976. After engineering roles at Plessey and D.G. Nash, he spent June–December 1980 at CERN building ENQUIRE before later returning to invent the Web.
family_context_summary: Born 8 June 1955 in London to mathematicians/computer scientists Conway Berners-Lee and Mary Lee Woods (Berners-Lee), both of whom worked on the Ferranti Mark 1, the first commercially built computer.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were professional computer scientists/mathematicians on the Ferranti Mark 1 team, giving unusually direct early immersion in computing culture and ideas.
evidence_summary: Berners-Lee grew up in a household of professional computer pioneers, attended selective schooling, and took a first in physics at Oxford. Industry software engineering preceded a 1980 CERN contract where, at 25, he designed and implemented ENQUIRE. That hypertext prototype plus later CERN return produced the 1989 Web proposal. Family domain advantage is unusually clear; WWW fame itself arrived after age 26.
starting_point: Born in London in 1955 to Ferranti Mark 1 computer pioneers Conway Berners-Lee and Mary Lee Woods; raised with early computing conversation and selective UK schooling.
current_position: Inventor of the World Wide Web; professorial research fellow at Oxford, MIT professor emeritus, W3C director emeritus; continues advocacy for an open web (Solid/Inrupt); living as of 2025–2026.

trajectory.event: Earned a first-class degree in physics from The Queen's College, Oxford.
At CERN, proposed a hypertext system and built the ENQUIRE prototype for sharing research information.
Submitted the World Wide Web information-management proposal at CERN.
Implemented the first web browser/editor and web server; published the first website.
Founded the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) at MIT to standardize the Web.
Knighted by Queen Elizabeth II for services to the global development of the Internet.
Received the ACM Turing Award for inventing the World Wide Web and its core protocols.

name: Trevor Blackwell
milestone_by_age_26: Joined Viaweb in September 1995 at age 25 during his Harvard CS PhD and wrote core image-rendering, order-processing, and statistics software for the pioneering web-based online store platform later acquired by Yahoo.
early_history_summary: Raised in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, Blackwell earned a BEng from Carleton University in 1992 and began a Harvard CS PhD (1993–1998). Midway through graduate school he joined Paul Graham and Robert Morris at Viaweb, becoming a key engineer on early e-commerce software before the 1998 Yahoo acquisition.
family_context_summary: Grew up in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, Canada; detailed parental occupations and wealth are not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Blackwell's age-26 milestone is core engineering on Viaweb at 25 alongside Graham and Morris—an elite technical peer set riding the mid-1990s web-commerce wave. Harvard PhD training supplied scarce systems skills; family background is thinly documented. Later founding of Anybots and co-founding Y Combinator (2005) amplified the Viaweb network into lasting platform power.
starting_point: Born 1969 in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan; engineering undergraduate at Carleton before Harvard CS PhD—family class details not documented.
current_position: Y Combinator co-founder (listed as Founder, Retired); roboticist and former Anybots CEO; continues robotics/startup-related work; living as of mid-2020s.

trajectory.event: Completed Bachelor of Engineering at Carleton University.
Joined Viaweb and built image rendering, order processing, and statistics software for early web storefronts.
Completed Harvard CS PhD; Viaweb was acquired by Yahoo and he led Yahoo Store development.
Founded Anybots to build teleoperated humanoid robots.
Co-founded Y Combinator with Paul Graham, Jessica Livingston, and Robert Morris.
Anybots announced a humanoid robot that balances and walks without oversized feet for stability.

name: Terry A. Davis
milestone_by_age_26: TempleOS and related public recognition emerged in the mid-2000s to 2010s (well after age 26); by age 26 he had an ASU master's (1994, age ~24) and Ticketmaster engineering work, which are ordinary early-career steps rather than a material public milestone.

After onset of severe mental illness in 1996 he later built TempleOS alone.
family_context_summary: Born in West Allis, Wisconsin, seventh of eight children; father was an industrial engineer. Family moved across several U.S. states.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an industrial engineer; early home computing access included school Apple II and a Commodore 64 as a teenager.
evidence_summary: Fame and the TempleOS body of work post-date age 26; MS degree and Ticketmaster employment do not clear the material-milestone bar used for this dataset.

name: Jan Leike

early_history_summary: German-trained in math/CS (Freiburg undergrad/master's), Leike earned a 2016 PhD in reinforcement learning under Marcus Hutter at ANU, did a short FHI postdoc, then worked on alignment at DeepMind and OpenAI (Head of Alignment / Superalignment co-lead) before joining Anthropic in 2024.
evidence_summary: TIME (2023) listed him as 36 → birth ~1987; PhD 2016 is past age 26. Early PhD years alone without a dated breakout product, founding, or award by 26 do not qualify.
